## Appendix A Some Mathematics

There are a number of mathematical ideas that underpin the analysis in the main text. To provide a self-contained introduction to this circle of ideas, we summarize some of them in this appendix. In particular, ideas from projective geometry, positive geometry, twisted cohomology, and hyperplane arrangements appear in various places in the text, and formalizing these concepts sheds some light on the arenas in which they appear.

### A.1 Projective Geometry

Many of the geometric constructions considered in the main text are most naturally considered in projective space.2828 28 For general introductions to projective geometry, see e.g. [99, 100, 101]. Projective $n$ -space, ${\mathbb{P}}^{n}$ , is the space of all lines through the origin in $n+1$ dimensions.2929 29 This can be any vector space, but we will mainly consider real projective space, which is the space of lines through the origin in ${\mathbb{R}}^{n+1}$ . Broadly speaking, projective space is useful when thinking about any question that does not explicitly involve distances, volumes, or other dimensionful measures. In particular, questions of incidence—like whether a given point is on a given line, or determining the intersection point between two lines—are naturally formulated and answered projectively.

#### Projective space:

As an example, ${\mathbb{P}}^{1}$ is the space of all lines through the origin in ${\mathbb{R}}^{2}$ . We can specify a point on the projective line by the pair

$$ \left(\begin{array}[]{c}y\\
x\end{array}\right)\sim t\left(\begin{array}[]{c}y\\
x\end{array}\right), $$

where $\sim$ indicates that we should identify vectors that differ by an overall rescaling. A convenient way to label the points is by their intersection with some reference line:

$$  $$

For concreteness, we have taken the line $y=1$ . This is equivalent to using the rescaling freedom to fix the top component of the lines in (A.1) to be $1$ ; rescalings are equivalent to sliding the red line up and down. Notice that this coordinatization obviously misses the $x$ -axis, which does not intersect the red line. This “line at infinity” can be covered by choosing a different reference line.

Two-dimensional projective space ${\mathbb{P}}^{2}$ has more interesting features. This is the space of lines through the origin in three-dimensions, which we can write as

$$ X^{I}=\Bigg(\begin{array}[]{c}z\\[-4.0pt]
x\\[-4.0pt]
y\end{array}\Bigg)\,,\quad{\rm with}\quad X^{I}\sim tX^{I}\,. $$

As before, we can coordinatize ${\mathbb{P}}^{2}$ by labeling lines by their intersection points with some reference plane. It is convenient to take the plane $z=1$ . This projective space is therefore similar to the ordinary Euclidean plane, with the addition of a “line at infinity” that is missed by any particular choice of coordinates. What the coordinatization (A.2) makes manifest is the SL $(3)$ invariance of projective space, which maps lines in the projective plane into other lines. The ${\mathbb{R}^{2}}\rtimes$ SL $(2)$ subgroup is the obvious set of affine linear transformations, which maps a plane vector as $\vec{x}\mapsto{\mathbb{L}}\,\vec{x}+\vec{t}$ , with ${\mathbb{L}}$ an SL $(2)$ matrix and $\vec{t}$ a vector. The SL $(3)$ group then acts as

$$ \Bigg(\begin{array}[]{c}z\\[-4.0pt]
x\\[-4.0pt]
y\end{array}\Bigg)=\ \left(\begin{array}[]{cc}c&\,\penalty\ \vec{b}\\[4.0pt]
\vec{t}&\,\penalty\ {\mathbb{L}}\end{array}\right)\Bigg(\begin{array}[]{c}z\\[-4.0pt]
x\\[-4.0pt]
y\end{array}\Bigg)\,, $$

with $\vec{b}$ a vector and $c$ a constant. Using our rescaling freedom to set $z=1$ , performing an SL $(3)$ transformation (A.3) and then re-fixing the gauge $z=1$ , we find that the SL $(3)$ acts nonlinearly on a vector in the projective plane:

$$ \vec{x}\mapsto\frac{{\mathbb{L}}\,\vec{x}+\vec{t}}{\vec{b}\cdot\vec{x}+c}\,. $$

We see that the choice of a line at infinity causes the SL $(3)$ to be realized on the coordinates nonlinearly because it does not leave the line at infinity invariant.3030 30 The affine group ${\mathbb{R}^{2}}\rtimes$ SL $(2)$ is precisely the subgroup that maps points on the line at infinity to other points on the same line. One can require further structures to be left invariant, and this will further reduce the symmetry group (for example, fixing two points on the line at infinity reduces the symmetries to the $(1+1)d$ Poincaré group). Klein’s Erlangen program was essentially to proceed in this way and classify geometries by the subset of projective transformations that they preserve.

Projective space is well adapted to ask questions of incidence, so let’s see how this works. Recall that points in ${\mathbb{P}}^{2}$ can be represented as $X^{I}$ , with a raised index, as in (A.2). We can therefore represent a line in projective space as

$$ L_{I}X^{I}\equiv Ax+By+Cz=0\,. $$

Using the rescaling freedom to set $z=1$ reproduces the usual formula for a line, $Ax+By+C=0$ . It is convenient to associate lines to the coefficients $L_{I}$ , with a lowered index. The only tensor that is invariant under the SL $(3)$ symmetries of projective space is the Levi–Civita symbol $\epsilon_{IJK}$ . Given two points $X_{1}^{I}$ and $X_{2}^{J}$ , we can then construct the line that connects them as

$$ L_{I}^{(12)}=\epsilon_{IJK}X_{1}^{J}X_{2}^{K}\,. $$

The antisymmetry of the Levi–Civita symbol makes it clear that $L_{I}^{(12)}X_{1}^{I}=L_{I}^{(12)}X_{2}^{I}=0$ , so that both the points $X_{1}$ and $X_{2}$ are on the line, as desired. It is straightforward to check whether a third point $Y^{I}$ is on the line by checking whether

$$ L_{I}^{(12)}Y^{I}=\epsilon_{IJK}Y^{I}X_{1}^{J}X_{2}^{K}\overset{?}{=}0\,. $$

Similarly, given two lines $L^{1}_{I}$ and $L^{2}_{J}$ , their intersection point $X^{I}_{(12)}$ is

$$ X^{I}_{(12)}=\epsilon^{IJK}L^{1}_{J}L^{2}_{K}\,. $$

Note that, in all of these examples, the lines and points are the only things that we can construct from the objects at hand with the right index structure. For example, three points all lie on a line if

$$ \epsilon_{IJK}X_{1}^{I}X_{2}^{J}X_{3}^{K}\equiv\langle X_{1}X_{2}X_{3}\rangle=0\,, $$

and three lines meet at a point if

$$ \epsilon^{IJK}L^{1}_{I}L^{2}_{J}L^{3}_{K}\equiv\langle L_{1}L_{2}L_{3}\rangle=0\,. $$

Another nice feature of projective space is that all pairs of lines intersect somewhere, even parallel ones. From the perspective of the projective plane, parallel lines meet on the line at infinity.3131 31 We can see this explicitly by considering the two lines $L^{1}_{I}X^{I}=Ax+By+C=0$ and $L^{2}_{I}X^{I}=Ax+By+C^{\prime}=0$ . Their intersection point is then

$$ X_{(12)}^{I}=\epsilon^{IJK}L^{1}_{J}L^{2}_{k}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\ A(C-C^{\prime})\\ B(C-C^{\prime})\end{array}\right). $$

(A.11) Recall that points with $z=0$ do not intersect the plane $z=1$ , and so lie at infinity. More generally, we can think of the gauge where we set $z=1$ as covering the parts of ${\mathbb{P}}^{2}$ for which $X^{I}L_{I}^{\infty}\neq 0$ , with

$$ L_{I}^{\infty}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}1\\ 0\\ 0\end{array}\right). $$

(A.12) This coordinate chart therefore covers all points that do not lie on the line at infinity.

We can also consider more complicated structures in projective space. For example, we can express a conic $Ax^{2}+Bxy+Cy^{2}+Dx+Ey+F=0$ as $C_{IJ}X^{I}X^{J}=0$ . Note that $C_{IJ}$ has $5$ independent components after modding out by the overall rescaling freedom, so any five points determine a conic that passes through them. It is then possible to use similar techniques to construct various tangents to and points on the conic. For example, one can prove Pascal’s Theorem, which states that if $6$ points happen to lie on a conic, if we look at the inscribed hexagon obtained by connecting these points pairwise, then the three intersection points of opposing sides will lie on a single line.

An interesting feature of projective space is so-called projective duality. In the context of ${\mathbb{P}}^{2}$ , it is particularly easy to see: we have assigned points as $X^{I}$ with raised indices and lines as $L_{I}$ with lowered indices, but clearly nothing changes if we swap every raised index into a lowered one, and vice versa. This implies that any projective statement involving points and lines continues to be true if we everywhere interchange the words points and lines. As an example, the projective dual of Pascal’s theorem is Brianchon’s theorem, which states that if six lines inscribe a conic, then the lines formed by connecting opposite vertices of the hexagon will meet at a point.

We can also consider higher-dimensional projective spaces, where planes are now associated to objects with additional indices. For example, in ${\mathbb{P}}^{3}$ , points are labeled by $X^{I}$ , planes are labeled by $H_{I}$ (or equivalently antisymmetric tensors $H^{IJK}$ ) and lines correspond to antisymmetric tensors $L^{IJ}$ . The invariant tensor is now $\epsilon_{IJKL}$ , and we can use a similar logic to the ${\mathbb{P}}^{2}$ case to see that just like two points determine a line, two planes intersect along a line. In ${\mathbb{P}}^{n}$ , a $(p-1)$ -plane corresponds to an antisymmetric tensor $H^{I_{1}\cdots I_{p}}$ , or equivalently $H_{J_{1}\cdots J_{n+1-p}}$ if we use the invariant tensor $\epsilon_{I_{1}\cdots I_{n+1}}$ to lower the indices. In general dimensions, projective duality interchanges $p$ -planes and $(n-p-1)$ -planes.

#### Volumes:

Although there is no notion of volume in projective space, it is nevertheless often useful to think about volumes projectively. This requires introducing some additional structure in the form of a line/plane at infinity $L^{\infty}_{I}$ . We can then construct volumes in a projectively invariant way.

For example, in ${\mathbb{P}}^{1}$ , we define volumes by choosing a point at infinity $Y^{I}=(1,0)$ . It is then natural to describe the points (A.1) in the chart that sets $y=1$ . We can then write the length of the interval between the points $X_{a}^{I}$ and $X_{b}^{J}$ as

$$ L=\frac{\langle X_{a}X_{b}\rangle}{\langle YX_{a}\rangle\langle YX_{b}\rangle}\,, $$

where $\langle X_{a}X_{b}\rangle\equiv\epsilon_{IJ}X_{a}^{I}X_{b}^{J}$ . Notice that despite the fact that the choice of a point at infinity breaks the symmetries of projective space down to those of the affine line, it is still possible to write the length of an interval in a way that respects the scaling invariance of projective space. If we re-scale all the coordinates $X$ by the same amount, the expression (A.13) is invariant.

We can also talk about volumes in ${\mathbb{P}}^{2}$ . In this case the most relevant example will be the area of a triangle. Given three points $X_{1}^{I},X_{2}^{J},X_{3}^{K}$ , the area of the triangle defined by these points can be written as

$$ A=\frac{\langle X_{1}X_{2}X_{3}\rangle}{(L^{\infty}\cdot X_{1})(L^{\infty}\cdot X_{2})(L^{\infty}\cdot X_{3})}\,, $$

which involves a choice of line at infinity, which it is often convenient to choose to be (A.12). We can also define the area of a triangle in terms of the lines that define it, rather than the points that are its vertices. Imagine that a triangle is bounded by the lines $L^{a}_{I},L^{b}_{J},L^{c}_{K}$ . The area of this triangle then is

$$ A=\frac{\langle L^{a}L^{b}L^{c}\rangle^{2}}{\langle L^{\infty}L^{a}L^{b}\rangle\langle L^{\infty}L^{b}L^{c}\rangle\langle L^{\infty}L^{c}L^{a}\rangle}\,, $$

which is the only way to build an invariant out of these objects with the correct scaling weight.

In higher dimensions, it is also easy to write expressions for the volumes of simplices. Given a plane at infinity $H_{I}^{\infty}$ , the volume of a simplex in ${\mathbb{P}}^{N}$ with vertices $X_{1},\cdots X_{N+1}$ is

$$ V=\frac{\langle X_{1}\cdots X_{N+1}\rangle}{(H^{\infty}\cdot X_{1})\cdots(H^{\infty}\cdot X_{N+1})}\,. $$

Similarly, if we define a simplex via the $N+1$ hyperplanes $H_{I}^{a}$ that bound it, we can write its volume as

$$ V=\frac{\langle 1\cdots(n+1)\rangle^{N}}{\langle\infty\,1\cdots n\rangle\cdots\langle\infty\,2\cdots(n+1)\rangle}\,, $$

where we have used the shorthand of replacing a plane with its label inside the brackets.

#### Differential forms:

In the main text, we study families of integrals of differential forms that live on ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ minus some singular divisors corresponding to a hyperplane arrangement. It is often useful to describe these differential forms projectively, so we now want to consider how to write differential (top) forms on projective space.

We first consider one-dimensional projective space ${\mathbb{P}}^{1}$ . Naively, any form built from $X$ and ${\rm d}X$ would be acceptable as long as it is invariant under overall re-scalings of $X$ . Hoewever, in order for differential forms to be well-defined, they must actually be invariant under local GL $(1)$ rescalings that send $X^{I}\mapsto t(X)X^{I}$ . This means that a well-defined differential form on ${\mathbb{P}}^{1}$ will be writeable as $\langle X{\rm d}X\rangle f(X)$ , where $f$ is a function of weight $-2$ under local rescalings. As a concrete example, consider two points $X_{a}$ and $X_{b}$ . It is possible to construct a well-defined projectively invariant differential form as

$$ \Omega=\frac{\langle ab\rangle\langle X{\rm d}X\rangle}{\langle Xa\rangle\langle Xb\rangle}\,. $$

We can write this form more explicitly by choosing a coordinate chart where

$$ X^{I}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}1\\
x\end{array}\right),\quad{\rm d}X^{I}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}0\\
{\rm d}x\end{array}\right),\quad X^{I}_{a}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}1\\
a\end{array}\right),\quad X^{I}_{b}=\left(\begin{array}[]{c}1\\
b\end{array}\right), $$

so that (A.18) is

$$ \Omega_{1}=\frac{(b-a){\rm d}x}{(x-a)(x-b)}\,. $$

The construction in a general projective space ${\mathbb{P}}^{n}$ is quite similar: forms can be written as $\Omega=\langle X{\rm d}X\cdots{\rm d}X\rangle f(X)$ , which involves $n$ different ${\rm d}X$ s and where $f(X)$ has scaling weight $-(n+1)$ . For example, given three lines in ${\mathbb{P}}^{2}$ forming a triangle, the natural differential form is

$$ \Omega_{2}=\frac{\langle X{\rm d}X{\rm d}X\rangle\langle L_{1}L_{2}L_{3}\rangle}{(L_{1}\cdot X)(L_{2}\cdot X)(L_{3}\cdot X)}\,. $$

More generally, given a simplex in ${\mathbb{P}}^{n}$ (built from $n+1$ hyperplanes), the following top form can be constructed3232 32 Note that in the main text—in particular in Section 4—we continue to denote hyperplanes by $L_{a,I}$ , like lines, and write projective coordinates as $P^{I}$ in order to not cause confusion with the kinematic variables $X_{i}$ .

$$ \Omega_{n+1}=\frac{\langle X{\rm d}X\cdots{\rm d}X\rangle\langle H_{1}H_{2}\cdots H_{n+1}\rangle}{(H_{1}\cdot X)(H_{2}\cdot X)\cdots(H_{n+1}\cdot X)}\,. $$

We will now see that these differential forms have the interpretation of canonical forms for the corresponding simplicial positive geometries.

### A.2 Canonical Forms

The concept of canonical forms has played an important role in defining our basis of integrals in the main text. In this section, we will give a pedagogical introduction to canonical forms for readers who haven’t come across them before.

Canonical forms are naturally associated to positive geometries [92]. Roughly speaking, a positive geometry is a convex region with boundaries of all codimension (which themselves are lower-dimensional positive geometries), with a distinguished top-dimensional form called its canonical form. For our purposes, it will suffice to consider a region whose boundaries are hyperplanes (meaning, linear functions of the coordinates).3333 33 The canonical form exists for more complicated positive regions, depending on the genus of the curve parametrizing the boundary. For example, in two dimensions, the boundary may be a conic section cut by lines. We do not use canonical forms in this broader sense throughout the text, but see [92] for more details. The canonical form associated with this region is the unique form with logarithmic singularities along all its boundaries (and nowhere else), whose residue on the boundaries is the canonical form of the lower-dimensional positive geometry. Throughout this paper, we choose the residues at the vertices of the bounded regions to be $\pm 1$ , which fixes the canonical form up to an overall sign (or orientation).

It is best to illustrate the meaning of canonical forms by looking at examples:

- • Interval: Consider the following bounded interval in one dimension: $x$ $-b$ $-a$ We would like to define a one-form on this interval with logarithmic singularities only at the endpoints $x=-a$ and $x=-b$ . Clearly, this form must be a linear combination of ${\rm d}x/(x+a)$ and ${\rm d}x/(x+b)$ . It seems that we can set the residues to be whatever we wish. However, requiring that there are no singularities anywhere else imposes a restriction, as both of these forms, on their own, also have a singularity at infinity. In order to cancel such a singularity (also logarithmic), we must subtract the two terms; i.e. the residues at $-a$ and $-b$ must be equal in magnitude, but have opposite signs. Taking the residues to have unit magnitudes fixes the canonical form on the interval up to an overall sign:

$$ \Omega=\frac{{\rm d}x}{x+a}-\frac{{\rm d}x}{x+b}=\frac{(b-a)\,{\rm d}x}{(x+a)(x+b)}={\rm d}\log\left(\frac{x+a}{x+b}\right). $$

(A.23) We used this result in Section 3.2. Notice also that this canonical form can be written in a projectively invariant way as in (A.20).

- • Triangle: Next, we move to bounded regions in two dimensions. We start with the example of a triangle. For simplicity, we take two of its lines to coincide with the coordinate axes, $L_{1}=x_{1}$ and $L_{2}=x_{2}$ , and the third line, $L_{3}=a_{1}x_{1}+a_{2}x_{2}+a_{3}$ , to be generic: $x_{1}$ $x_{2}$ $L_{2}$ $L_{1}$ $L_{3}$ A natural guess for the canonical form on this triangle is

$$ \Omega=\frac{{\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2}}{L_{1}L_{2}L_{3}}\,, $$

(A.24) which is correct up to normalization. A nice feature is that the properly-normalized canonical form associated to a triangle can be expressed as the projectively invariant form (A.21), which reduces to (A.24) up to normalization after choosing a coordinate chart. Besides having the correct singularities on the codimension-one boundaries, the form (A.24) does a bit more, which goes at the heart of the definition of a canonical form. Consider taking the limit $L_{1}=x_{1}\to 0$ , i.e. going to the boundary defined by $L_{1}$ . The residue of (A.24) at this locus is

$$ {\rm Res}[\Omega]\Big|_{L_{1}=0}=\frac{1}{a_{2}}\frac{{\rm d}x_{2}}{x_{2}(x_{2}+a_{3}/a_{2})}\,, $$

(A.25) which, up to an overall factor, is the canonical form on the interval $[-a_{3}/a_{2},0]$ ; cf. (A.23). Sending $\Omega\to a_{3}\Omega$ , would then also fix the correct normalization of the form. (For a generic non-right triangle, the precise normalization factor will be different.) We have just displayed an important general feature of canonical forms: the residue of a canonical form on any of its boundaries is the canonical form of the boundary. The result (A.24) can also be written as

$$ \Omega={\rm d}\log\left(\frac{L_{1}}{L_{2}}\right)\wedge{\rm d}\log\left(\frac{L_{2}}{L_{3}}\right), $$

(A.26) which is independent of the choice of repeated line (despite the apparent asymmetry among the lines).

- • Quadrilateral: As a more nontrivial example, consider a quadrilateral bounded by four lines $\{L_{i}=0\}$ . It is tempting to guess that the canonical form is

$$ \Omega\stackrel{{\scriptstyle?}}{{=}}\frac{{\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2}}{L_{1}L_{2}L_{3}L_{4}}\,. $$

(A.27) This time, however, this guess is wrong. It is easy to understand this by looking at the drawing: $x_{1}$ $x_{2}$ $L_{1}$ $L_{4}$ $L_{2}$ $L_{3}$ $L_{N}$ In the limit $L_{1}\to 0$ , the residue of the canonical form should give the canonical form on the bounded interval contained by the line $L_{1}$ . However, the ansatz in (A.27) also contains a spurious pole at $L_{1}=0\cap L_{4}=0$ , which lies outside of our bounded region! A similar reasoning implies that there is another spurious pole when $L_{2}\to 0\cap L_{3}\to 0$ . To fix this, we must add something to the numerator of (A.27) which offsets these unwanted poles. The minimal way of removing both poles is to include a numerator that is linear in the coordinates. It is the line $L_{N}$ connecting the white dots in the figure above. Thus, up to an overall normalization (which we can include in the definition of $L_{N}$ ), we obtain

$$ \Omega=\frac{L_{N}\,{\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2}}{L_{1}L_{2}L_{3}L_{4}}\,. $$

(A.28) Below we will discuss a property of canonical forms—triangulation independence—that explains why the numerator is a line in this example (and not a more complicated curve).

- • Pentagon: A pentagon is determined by five lines $\{L_{i}=0\}$ , which intersect at 10 different points: $x_{1}$ $x_{2}$ $L_{1}$ $L_{2}$ $L_{3}$ $L_{4}$ $L_{5}$ $C_{N}$ Five of these points are the vertices of the pentagon and the five other points lie outside of it. As in the previous example, the absence of spurious poles at the intersections outside the pentagon fixes the numerator of the canonical form associated to the pentagon. There exists a unique conic $C_{N}$ passing through any given five points on the plane. We pick the conic section going through all spurious poles to be the numerator of the canonical form:

$$ \Omega=\frac{C_{N}\,{\rm d}x_{1}\wedge{\rm d}x_{2}}{L_{1}L_{2}L_{3}L_{4}L_{5}}\,. $$

(A.29)

- • Polygons: For general polygons, it is often simpler to determine the canonical forms by triangulation. The canonical form of a polygon is the sum of canonical forms of the triangles in a triangulation [92].3434 34 The generalization to higher dimensions is the obvious one: that the canonical form of a polytope is the sum of those of the simplices in a triangulation. The uniqueness property of canonical forms guarantees that any triangulation will give the same answer. The only important step is to cancel residues from the lines used to glue the triangles together, as these correspond to spurious singularities. This also explains why the degree of the numerator increases with the number of sides of the polygon. As we need to glue more triangles together, when putting everything under a common denominator, we form a numerator of higher and higher degree.

- • Simplices: The generalization of a triangle in higher dimensions is a simplex. It consists of the intersection of $d+1$ hyperplanes in $d$ dimensions. If we parametrize the equations of the hyperplanes as $L_{i}=H_{i}\cdot X$ , with $X$ being the projective coordinates on ${\mathbb{R}}^{d}$ , then the canonical form of a simplex is (A.22). Upon choosing the section $\{X_{i}=x_{i},X_{d+1}=1\}$ , this can be written as

$$ \Omega=\frac{|H_{1}\cdots H_{d+1}|}{L_{1}\cdots L_{d+1}}\,{\rm d}x_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge{\rm d}x_{d}\,, $$

(A.30) where the numerator is the determinant of the matrix built out of the coefficients of all hyperplanes, which fixes the normalization for the simplex to have unit residues at the corners. For the case of the triangle discussed above, picking two of the lines to be parallel to the coordinate axes gives $|H_{1}H_{2}H_{3}|=a_{3}$ .

In higher dimensions, and for a larger number of hyperplanes, the bounded regions become harder to visualize and it is more difficult to build the canonical form of a given polytope in a systematic way. With the examples listed above, one should have enough intuition to determine the canonical forms of general hyperplane arrangements by either triangulation or educated guesswork. A deeper dive into the subject and some of its applications can be found in [92, 78].

### A.3 Twisted Cohomology

In this section, we give a brief account of twisted de Rham cohomology, focusing on results needed in the main text. More comprehensive expositions can be found in the classic books [102, 103] and the reviews [84, 104, 105, 74]. Recent applications to the study of various aspects of Feynman integrals include [106, 107, 108, 109].

#### Twisted integrals:

Let $\mathbb{C}^{n}$ be $n$ -dimensional complex space. We are interested in integrals of forms defined on this space, which we will allow to be singular on a set of hypersurfaces defined by the polynomial equations $f_{i}(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})=0$ , for $i=1,\ldots,m$ . The union of these hypersurfaces is the divisor $D$ . In order to understand the space of possible integrals, we will therefore be interested in the cohomology of differential forms on the space $M\equiv\mathbb{C}^{n}\setminus D$ .

Consider differential $n$ -forms $\Omega$ , which are holomorphic on $M$ , but may be singular on the divisor, and so take the form

$$ \Omega=\frac{N(z)}{f_{1}^{p_{1}}\cdots f_{m}^{p_{m}}}\,{\rm d}z_{1}\wedge\cdots\wedge{\rm d}z_{n}\,,\quad $$

where $N(z)$ is a polynomial in $z=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n})$ and $p_{i}$ are integers. In general, we are then interested in twisted integrals of the form

$$ I\equiv\int_{\gamma}\Omega\,\prod_{i=1}^{m}f_{i}(z)^{\varepsilon_{i}}\,, $$

with $\gamma$ some $n$ -dimensional integration domain. The twist parameters $\varepsilon_{i}$ appearing in (A.32) are not integers ( $\varepsilon_{i}\in{\mathbb{C}}\setminus{\mathbb{Z}}$ ), so the integrand is in general multivalued. We want to understand how many independent integrals there are of the form (A.32). We begin with a reminder of the concept of ordinary (de Rham) cohomology of differential forms and then explain how it generalizes to twisted cohomology.

#### de Rham complex:

When all the $\varepsilon_{i}=0$ (and on a suitable integration domain without a boundary), the answer to this question is provided by de Rham cohomology, which counts equivalence classes of integrands. In particular, since $\partial\gamma=0$ , Stokes’ theorem implies that $I$ will not change if we shift $\Omega\to\Omega+{\rm d}\xi$ , with $\xi$ an arbitrary $(n-1)$ -form. Two $n$ -forms are therefore equivalent upon integration if they only differ by the exterior derivative of a $(n-1)$ -form:

$$ \Omega\sim\Omega+{\rm d}\xi\,. $$

The vector space of such equivalence classes is precisely the de Rham cohomology group $H^{n}(M)$ , and so we see that the independent integrals of the form $I$ are in one-to-one correspondence with nontrivial cocycles in the de Rham cohomology.

#### Twisted de Rham complex:

In this paper, we are instead interested in integrals of the form (A.32), with nontrivial twist factors

$$ u\equiv\prod_{i=1}^{m}f_{i}(z)^{\varepsilon_{i}}\,. $$

The integration domain $\gamma$ now may have a boundary contained in the divisor $D$ , as long as the twist factor $u$ vanishes sufficiently quickly on $\partial\gamma$ . Stokes’ theorem then implies that

$$ \int_{\gamma}{\rm d}(u\xi)=\int_{\partial\gamma}u\xi=0\,. $$

This can also be written as

$$ \int_{\gamma}{\rm d}(u\xi)=\int_{\gamma}({\rm d}u\wedge\xi+u\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\xi)=\int_{\gamma}u\,({\rm d}+{\rm d}\log u\hskip 1.0pt\wedge)\xi\equiv\int_{\gamma}u\nabla_{\omega}\hskip 1.0pt\xi=0\,, $$

where we have introduced the covariant derivative

$$ \nabla_{\omega}\equiv{\rm d}+\omega\,\wedge\,, $$

defined in terms of the closed, holomomorphic $1$ -form

$$ \omega\equiv{\rm d}\log u=\sum_{i=1}^{m}\varepsilon_{i}\frac{{\rm d}f_{i}}{f_{i}}\,. $$

Two rational forms then yield equivalent integrals if they differ by the covariant derivative of a $(n-1)$ -form:

$$ \Omega\sim\Omega+\nabla_{\omega}\hskip 1.0pt\xi\,. $$

The set of equivalence classes of forms $\Omega$ with respect to the twisted differential (A.37) then defines the twisted (de Rham) cohomology group $H^{n}_{\omega}(M,\nabla_{\omega})={\rm Ker}\nabla_{\omega}/{\rm Im}\nabla_{\omega}$ . This cohomology provides a basis of independent rational integrands $\Omega$ appearing in (A.32) and hence defines the space of independent master integrals.

#### A simple example:

It is worthwhile to illustrate the above considerations with a simple example. One important lesson is that twisting an integral typically reduces the dimensionality of the cohomology.

Consider the space of forms defined on $M=\mathbb{C}\setminus\{0,-1,\infty\}$ (that is, the complex line minus three points). In ordinary cohomology, the space of holomorphic $1$ -forms is spanned by

$$ \Omega_{1}\equiv\frac{{\rm d}z}{z}\,,\quad\Omega_{2}\equiv\frac{{\rm d}z}{z+1}\,. $$

It is easy to check that all other holomorphic $1$ -forms in this space can be reduced to a linear combination of those two forms, plus total derivatives. For example,

$$ \frac{{\rm d}z}{z^{2}(z+1)^{3}}=3\Omega_{2}-3\Omega_{1}-{\rm d}\left(\frac{2+9z+6z^{2}}{2z(1+z^{2})}\right). $$

We therefore see that $\Omega_{1}$ and $\Omega_{2}$ act as a basis for the de Rham cohomology $H^{1}(M)$ .

Next, we consider the twisted cohomology defined by the twist function $u=z^{\varepsilon}$ . It is easy to see then that, inside the twisted integral, the one-form $\Omega_{1}$ becomes a total derivative

$$ \int u\hskip 1.0pt\Omega_{1}=\int z^{\varepsilon}\frac{{\rm d}z}{z}=\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\int{\rm d}(z^{\varepsilon})\,, $$

or, equivalently, we see that

$$ \Omega_{1}=\nabla_{\omega}\left(\frac{1}{\varepsilon}\right), $$

where $\omega=\varepsilon\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}z/z$ . As a result, the basis is now one-dimensional. In principle, we could have introduced more general twists, but for this one-dimensional problem, we always end up removing a single member of the basis (a specific linear combination of the two members of the ordinary de Rham basis, determined by our choice of twist function).

#### A vanishing theorem:

As we consider higher-dimensional examples, the space of integrals becomes seemingly much more complex, and the structure of twisted cohomology would seem forbiddingly complicated. However, Aomoto [86] proved a powerful statement that organizes our thinking about the problem. It turns out that for generic twists, only the $n$ -dimensional twisted cohomology is nonzero in an $n$ -dimensional space, i.e. $H^{k}_{\omega}(M,\nabla_{\omega})=0$ , for $n\neq k$ . This means that only $n$ -forms in $M$ are nontrivial.3535 35 In a complex space, the nontrivial cohomology is in holomorphic $n$ -forms, so they have half the total dimension, while in a real space, these are top-dimensional real $n$ -forms. An important consequence is that the dimension of the twisted cohomology is closely related to the Euler character of $M$ . In general, the Euler character is given by the sum of (signed) dimensions of the de Rham cohomology, but since only one of them is non-vanishing, we have [102]

$$ {\rm dim}\,H^{n}_{\omega}(M,\nabla_{\omega})=(-1)^{n}\chi(M)\,. $$

This result is particularly useful because it allows us to determine geometrically the dimension of the twisted cohomology of top forms ( $n$ -forms), and consequently the number of master integrals required to span the vector space of integrals. It turns out that the spaces $M$ of interest in this paper have sufficient structure that $\chi(M)$ can be computed by simple counting.

### A.4 Hyperplane Arrangements

The singularities of the integrals that arise in the computation of the FRW wavefunction have a particularly simple structure—compared to generic twisted integrals in (A.32)—in terms of hyperplane arrangements. In the following, we provide a bit of mathematical background on the theory of hyperplane arrangements (see [110, 111, 112] for more comprehensive treatments).

#### Definitions:

Recall that a hyperplane $H$ in an $n$ -dimensional vector space $V$ (for our purposes, typically ${\mathbb{C}}^{n}$ or ${\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ ) is an affine subspace of dimension $(n-1)$ defined by

$$ c_{1}z_{1}+\cdots+c_{n}z_{n}=a\,. $$

A finite set of such hyperplanes is the hyperplane arrangement ${\cal A}$ .3636 36 In general, both hyperplanes and hyperplane arrangements can be defined with respect to an arbitrary vector space over an arbitrary field. The rank of an arrangement is the dimension of the space spanned by the vectors normal to the hyperplanes, and an arrangement is called essential if it has maximal rank (i.e. the dimension of the ambient vector space).

#### Intersection, deletion, and restriction:

There are several natural operations one can perform on a hyperplane arrangement. The first is to consider the intersections of the hyperplanes that comprise an arrangement ${\cal A}$ . We denote the set of all such intersections by $L({\cal A})$ . This includes the ambient vector space $V$ itself, thought of as an intersection with the empty set. Note that $L({\cal A})$ has a natural partial order by reverse inclusion, so that $X\leq Y$ if $X\supseteq Y$ , for $X,Y\in L({\cal A})$ . The collection of a subset of the planes, ${\cal B}\subseteq{\cal A}$ , is called a subarrangement.

An important subarrangement of ${\cal A}$ is obtained by deletion, wherein we choose a distinguished hyperplane $H_{0}$ and remove it from the arrangement, producing a new arrangement.

Another natural operation is restriction. As in deletion, we choose a distinguished hyperplane, but now envision it as the ambient vector space of a hyperplane arrangement, and think of the intersections of all the other planes that intersect it as hyperplanes in this ambient space. In order to define this operation formally, we first have to develop some notation. Given an element $X\in L({\cal A})$ , we first define the subarrangement of planes that contain $X$ as

$$ {\cal A}_{X}\equiv\{H\in{\cal A}\,|\,X\subseteq H\}\,. $$

The restriction of ${\cal A}$ to $X$ is then given by

$$ {\cal A}^{X}\equiv\{X\cap H\neq\varnothing\,|\,H\in{\cal A}/{\cal A}_{X}\}\,. $$

The latter describes the set of hyperplanes in the space $X$ that arise from the intersection of the planes not in ${\cal A}_{X}$ with $X$ .

Given a hyperplane arrangement ${\cal A}$ and a choice of distinguished hyperplane $H_{0}\in{\cal A}$ , we can form a triple

$$ ({\cal A},{\cal A}/H_{0},{\cal A}^{H_{0}})\,, $$

which consists of the arrangement itself, the arrangement with $H_{0}$ deleted, and the arrangement obtained by restriction to $H_{0}$ (see Fig. 8). This procedure of deletion-restriction plays an important role in the combinatorics of hyperplane arrangements.

#### Regions:

One important feature of hyperplane arrangements is that they partition the vector space $V$ into various regions. We denote the number of regions by ${\cal R}({\cal A})$ . Some of the regions can be bounded and we denote their number by ${\cal B}({\cal A})$ . These bounded regions will play an important role in connecting hyperplane arrangements to twisted cohomology. The number of regions satisfy nice relations under deletion-restriction: Given a triple, the number of regions and bounded regions are related by3737 37 There is a small technical requirement on the bounded region relation, which is that the deletion operation should not change the rank of the hyperplane arrangement. In the case that it does, ${\cal B}({\cal A})$ is instead zero [111].

$$ \displaystyle{\cal R}({\cal A}) \displaystyle={\cal R}({\cal A}/H_{0})+{\cal R}({\cal A}^{H_{0}})\,, \displaystyle{\cal B}({\cal A}) \displaystyle={\cal B}({\cal A}/H_{0})+{\cal B}({\cal A}^{H_{0}})\,. $$

One can then use these formulas directly to compute the number of (bounded) regions recursively. In Figure 8, the number of (bounded) regions can simply be counted and the above relations are easily verified.

*Figure 8: Illustration of a hyperplane arrangement ${\cal A}$ with a distinguished hyperplane $H_{0}$ (left). Deleting $H_{0}$ gives the arrangement ${\cal A}/H_{0}$ (middle), while the restriction to $H_{0}$ is ${\cal A}^{H_{0}}$ (right). Note that the numbers of (bounded) regions in this triple of arrangements satisfy the relations (A.49) and (A.50). Concretely, we see that there are $11=7+4$ total regions in the arrangement ${\cal A}$ , and $3=1+2$ bounded regions.*

#### Poincaré polynomial:

In higher-dimensional examples, it typically becomes extremely hard to visualize the hyperplane arrangements, so that simply counting the (bounded) regions is not an option. Fortunately, there is a systematic way to proceed using the Poincaré polynomial, $\pi({\cal A},t)$ . Beyond this, the connection between the number or regions and the Poincaré polynomials serves as an important bridge between the combinatorics of hyperplane arrangements, topology, and twisted cohomology.

The Poincaré polynomial can be given a formal definition,3838 38 Explicitly, the Poincaré polynomial is defined by

$$ \pi({\cal A},t)=\sum_{X\,\in\,L}\mu(V,X)(-t)^{r(X)}\,, $$

(A.51) where the sum runs over all elements of the poset of intersections $L({\cal A})$ . Here, $r(X)$ is the rank of the element $X$ and $\mu(V,X)$ is the Möbius function, which satisfies $\displaystyle\mu(X,X)$ $\displaystyle=1\,,$ (A.52) $\displaystyle\sum_{X\leq Z\leq Y}\mu(Z,Y)$ $\displaystyle=0\,,\quad\text{if}\penalty\ X<Y\,,$ (A.53) for elements $X,Y,Z\in L({\cal A})$ . The definition is somewhat unwieldy when it comes to actual calculations and it is typically easier to use the formula (A.54). but, for our purposes, it is sufficient to note how it behaves under the operation of deletion-restriction. Given a triple of arrangements (A.48), we have [113, 110]

$$ \pi({\cal A},t)=\pi({\cal A}/H_{0},t)+t\,\pi({\cal A}^{H_{0}},t)\,. $$

Starting from the Poincaré polynomial of the empty arrangement, $\pi(\varnothing,t)=1$ , we can use this relation to recursively compute the polynomial of more complicated arrangements.

A remarkable feature of the Poincaré polynomial is that, for real arrangements, it counts both the total number of regions that the hyperplanes split $V$ into and the number of bounded regions (for an essential arrangement) [110, 112]:3939 39 The proof of this result is actually not too difficult. The basic idea is to note that both the number of regions and the Poincaré polynomial satisfy the same relation under the deletion-restriction operation. Since the formula (A.55) is true for the empty arrangement, it is then true generally.

$$ \displaystyle{\cal R}({\cal A}) \displaystyle=\pi({\cal A},1)\,, \displaystyle{\cal B}({\cal A}) \displaystyle=(-1)^{n}\pi({\cal A},-1)\,. $$

A priori, it may not obvious why this fact is of interest to us. However, the Poincaré polynomial is also a generating functional for Betti numbers, so that the Euler character of the hyperplane arrangement is

$$ \chi({\cal A})=\pi({\cal A},-1)\,. $$

Comparing this to (A.44), we see that the number of bounded regions also computes the dimension of the twisted cohomology on the space $M$ where the hyperplane arrangement ${\cal A}$ is the singular divisor! In many cases, we can therefore read off the number of master integrals geometrically by counting the number of bounded regions, or equivalently by computing $\pi({\cal A},-1)$ .

#### Counting bounded regions:

As a practical matter, it is often difficult to actually compute the Poincaré polynomial. However, there is a fascinating way to proceed. We instead consider a hyperplane arrangement over the finite field ${\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ . The cardinality of the complement of the hyperplane arrangement, $\lvert\overline{\cal A}\rvert_{p}$ , is then given by [112]4040 40 The proof again proceeds by noting that these quantities satisfy the same deletion-restriction relations.

$$ \lvert\overline{\cal A}\rvert_{p}=p^{n}\pi({\cal A},-p^{-1})\,. $$

We can therefore extract $\pi({\cal A},t)$ by performing the following computation. We consider a hyperplane arrangement over the finite field ${\mathbb{F}}_{p}$ corresponding to the lattice $({\mathbb{Z}}/p)^{n}$ , where $p$ is a prime number. We then remove from this lattice all points that are intersected by the hyperplanes. The resulting number of points—the size of the complement—is a function of the prime $p$ . It turns out that $\lvert\overline{\cal A}\rvert_{p}$ is a polynomial of degree $n$ , so determining its general form is just a matter of empirically evaluating and counting $\lvert\overline{\cal A}\rvert_{p}$ for a small set of primes. Given this result, we then have

$$ {\cal B}({\cal A})=\lvert\overline{\cal A}\rvert_{p=1}\,. $$

For the single exchange integral discussed in Section 3, for example, this procedure gives $\lvert\overline{\cal A}\rvert_{p}=p^{2}-5p+8$ , and so

$$ \pi({\cal A},t)=1+5t+8t^{2}\,. $$

As we can see from Figure 2, there are indeed $\pi({\cal A},1)=14$ total regions and $\pi({\cal A},-1)=4$ bounded regions. Since $\pi$ is a generating function for Betti numbers, its coefficients count the dimensions of de Rham cohomology. In this case, we have $\{1,5,8\}$ -dimensional spaces of $\{0,1,2\}$ -forms.

### A.5 The Hypergeometric Function

We can illustrate all of these mathematical constructions in a simple example: the hypergeometric function. This is also a toy example of the cosmological integrals considered in the main text.

Imagine that we are interested in computing the following integral

$$ I(X)=\int_{0}^{\infty}{\rm d}x\,\frac{x^{\varepsilon_{1}}}{(x+X)^{\varepsilon_{2}}(x+1)^{\varepsilon_{3}}}\,\frac{1}{x(x+X)}\,, $$

where $X$ is a real constant and $\varepsilon_{i}$ are independent twist parameters. We will now show that this integral is part of a finite-dimensional vector space of integrals, and therefore satisfies a differential equation.

#### Master integrals:

The first step is to enlarge the problem and think of (A.61) as an element of the following family of integrals

$$ I_{n_{1}n_{2}n_{3}}(X)\equiv\int\frac{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}x}^{\varepsilon_{1}}}{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}(x+X)}^{\varepsilon_{2}}{\color[rgb]{0.1719,0.6289,0.1719}(x+1)}^{\varepsilon_{3}}}\,\Omega\,,\qquad\Omega\equiv\frac{{\rm d}x}{{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}x^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}n_{1}}}}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}(x+X)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}n_{2}}}}{\color[rgb]{0.1719,0.6289,0.1719}(x+1)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}n_{3}}}}}\,, $$

where $n_{i}$ are positive integers, and we require $\varepsilon_{1}-n_{1}>-1$ , and $n_{2}+\varepsilon_{2}+n_{3}+\varepsilon_{3}+n_{1}-\varepsilon_{1}>1$ , in order for the integrals to converge. The integral in (A.61) corresponds to $I_{110}$ .

The integrals (A.62) can be evaluated explicitly for particular values of the parameters; for example, they evaluate to power laws when $\varepsilon_{2}=\varepsilon_{3}=0$ . We are, however, interested in the case where the twists $\varepsilon_{i}$ are generic. In that case, we can think of the integrands in (A.62) as rational functions twisted by factors with the same singularities. The locations of these singularities define a hyperplane arrangement, which in this case corresponds to points on the line:

$$  $$

As we have described above, the twisted integrals (A.62) form a finite-dimensional vector space whose size is given by the number of bounded regions enclosed by the singular loci, $x=\{0,-X,-1\}$ . We see from the hyperplane arrangement that there are two bounded intervals, and hence the basis for the family of integrals in (A.62) is two-dimensional.

A convenient choice of basis is given by the integrals arising from the twists times the canonical forms for the bounded intervals. As shown in Appendix A.2, the canonical forms associated with the intervals $[-1,-X]$ and $[-X,0]$ are

$$ \displaystyle\Omega_{1} \displaystyle\equiv\Omega_{[-X,0]}=\frac{X}{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{x}\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{(x+X)}}\,{\rm d}x\,, \displaystyle\Omega_{2} \displaystyle\equiv\Omega_{[-1,-X]}=\frac{(1-X)}{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}{(x+X)}\color[rgb]{0.1719,0.6289,0.1719}{(x+1)}}\,{\rm d}x\,, $$

and the canonical basis of integrals is therefore

$$ \vec{I}\equiv\left[\begin{array}[]{c}I_{1}\\
I_{2}\end{array}\right]=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{\varepsilon_{1}}}{(x+X)^{\varepsilon_{2}}(x+1)^{\varepsilon_{3}}}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}\Omega_{1}\\
\Omega_{2}\end{array}\right]. $$

Our original integral (A.61) is $I_{1}$ , but any integral of the form (A.62) can be written as a linear combination of $I_{1}$ and $I_{2}$ with $X$ -dependent coefficients.

#### Differential equation:

It is now mechanical to derive a first-order matrix differential equation satisfied by these basis integrals: if we differentiate $I_{1}$ or $I_{2}$ with respect to the parameter $X$ , we have to be able to write the result back in terms of $I_{1}$ and $I_{2}$ . This procedure is completely systematic, but in general can be somewhat tedious. It is at this point that our choice of using canonical forms to define the basis integrals pays off. The derivatives of canonical forms with respect to $X$ can be written as derivatives with respect to the integration variable $x$ . Concretely, we have

$$ \displaystyle\partial_{X}\Omega_{1} \displaystyle=-\partial_{x}\left(\frac{1}{X}{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{x}}\,\Omega_{1}\right)=-\partial_{x}\left(\frac{1}{1-X}{\color[rgb]{0.1719,0.6289,0.1719}{(x+1)}}\,\Omega_{2}\right), \displaystyle\partial_{X}\Omega_{2} \displaystyle=\partial_{x}\left(\frac{1}{X}{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{x}}\,\Omega_{1}\right)=\partial_{x}\left(\frac{1}{1-X}{\color[rgb]{0.1719,0.6289,0.1719}{(x+1)}}\,\Omega_{2}\right). $$

These formulas are the un-integrated analogues of (4.11). Using these relations, it is straightforward to use integration by parts to derive the matrix differential equation for ${\cal I}$ . For example, consider the derivative of the first basis integral

$$ \partial_{X}I_{1}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{\varepsilon_{1}}}{(x+X)^{\varepsilon_{2}}(x+1)^{\varepsilon_{3}}}\left(\partial_{X}\Omega_{1}-\frac{\varepsilon_{2}}{x+X}\,\Omega_{1}\right). $$

Using (A.65), we can write the first term as a derivative with respect to $x$ and then integrate by parts. This leads to

$$ \hskip-5.69046pt\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{\varepsilon_{1}}\,\partial_{X}\Omega_{1}}{(x+X)^{\varepsilon_{2}}(x+1)^{\varepsilon_{3}}}=\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{x^{\varepsilon_{1}}}{(x+X)^{\varepsilon_{2}}(x+1)^{\varepsilon_{3}}}\left(\frac{\varepsilon_{1}}{X}\,\Omega_{1}-\frac{\varepsilon_{3}}{1-X}\,\Omega_{2}-\frac{\varepsilon_{2}}{X}\frac{x}{x+X}\,\Omega_{1}\right). $$

The first two terms are already proportional to the basis elements $I_{1}$ and $I_{2}$ . The last term in (A.68) combines with the last term in (A.67) as

$$ -\frac{\varepsilon_{2}}{x+X}\,\Omega_{1}-\frac{\varepsilon_{2}}{X}\frac{x}{x+X}\,\Omega_{1}=-\frac{\varepsilon_{2}}{X}\,\Omega_{1}\,. $$

Putting everything together, we get

$$ \partial_{X}I_{1}=\frac{\varepsilon_{1}-\varepsilon_{2}}{X}I_{1}-\frac{\varepsilon_{3}}{1-X}I_{2}\,. $$

Notice that the right-hand side is proportional to the twist parameters. This is a consequence of the relations (A.65) and (A.66), which guarantee that we can always treat the derivatives on the canonical forms by integrating by parts, so that they act on the twisted points. Following the same recipe, the derivative of the second basis integral becomes

$$ \partial_{X}I_{2}=-\frac{\varepsilon_{1}}{X}I_{1}+\frac{\varepsilon_{2}+\varepsilon_{3}}{1-X}I_{2}\,. $$

Defining ${\rm d}\equiv{\rm d}X\,\partial_{X}$ , we can combine (A.70) and (A.71) into a single matrix equation

$$ {\rm d}\,\vec{I}=A\,\vec{I}\,, $$

where the connection matrix $A$ is

$$ A=\left(\left[\begin{matrix}1&0\\
-1&0\end{matrix}\right]\varepsilon_{1}+\left[\begin{matrix}-1&0\\
0&0\end{matrix}\right]\varepsilon_{2}\right){\rm d}\log X+\left(\left[\begin{matrix}0&0\\
0&-1\end{matrix}\right]\varepsilon_{2}+\left[\begin{matrix}0&1\\
0&-1\end{matrix}\right]\varepsilon_{3}\right){\rm d}\log(1-X)\,. $$

We see that $A$ is a sum of dlog forms, $A=\sum_{i}\alpha_{i}(\varepsilon)\,{\rm d}\log\Phi_{i}(X)$ , and hence satisfies ${\rm d}A=0$ , i.e. it is a flat connection. Acting with ${\rm d}$ on (A.72) gives ${\rm d}A+A\wedge A=0$ , so that $A\wedge A=0$ , which is a nontrivial constraint on the entries of $A$ . Finally, note that all nonzero entries of $A$ are $\pm 1$ . This is a consequence of the basis of canonical forms having unit residues.

#### Hypergeometric solution:

The solutions to (A.72) can be written in terms of the Gauss hypergeometric function ${}_{2}F_{1}$ . To see this, we combine (A.70) and (A.71) into a single second-order equation for $I_{1}$ (which is the original integral (A.61) that we want to compute). Defining $I_{1}(X)\equiv X\hat{I}_{1}(X)$ and $X\equiv 1-z$ , we find

$$ \partial_{z}^{2}\hat{I}_{1}+\frac{c-z(1+a+b)}{z(1-z)}\hskip 1.0pt\partial_{z}\hat{I}_{1}-\frac{ab}{z(1-z)}\hskip 1.0pt\hat{I}_{1}=0\,, $$

with the parameters

$$ \displaystyle a \displaystyle\equiv 1+\varepsilon_{2}\,, \displaystyle b \displaystyle\equiv 1+\varepsilon_{2}+\varepsilon_{3}-\varepsilon_{1}\,, \displaystyle c \displaystyle\equiv 1+\varepsilon_{2}+\varepsilon_{3}\,. $$

We recognize (A.74) as the hypergeometric differential equation whose solution is

$$ \hat{I}_{1}(z)\propto\,{}_{2}F_{1}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}a,\,b\\[-3.0pt]
c\end{array}\Big\rvert\,z\,\right]\,. $$

Evaluating $I_{1}$ for a specific value of $X$ fixes the overall normalization and we eventually get

$$ I_{1}(X)=\frac{\Gamma[1+\varepsilon_{2}+\varepsilon_{3}-\varepsilon_{1}]\Gamma[\varepsilon_{1}]}{\Gamma[1+\varepsilon_{2}+\varepsilon_{3}]}\,X\,{}_{2}F_{1}\left[\begin{array}[]{c}1+\varepsilon_{2}\ ,\,1+\varepsilon_{2}+\varepsilon_{3}-\varepsilon_{1}\\[-2.0pt]
1+\varepsilon_{2}+\varepsilon_{3}\end{array}\Big\rvert\,1-X\,\right]. $$

Of course, in this case, we could also have found this solution by identifying the original integral (A.61) with the integral representation of the hypergeometric function. The second basis integral $I_{2}$ is a linearly independent hypergeometric function with slightly different parameters. We won’t write its explicit form, but any other member of the hypergeometric family can be written as a linear combination of these two functions.

#### Gauss contiguous relations:

Since the vector space of functions is two-dimensional, any three elements of the integral family (A.62) must be linearly dependent. The resulting linear relations are the so-called contiguous relations of the hypergeometric function. They relate different ${}_{2}F_{1}$ functions with values of $\varepsilon_{1,2,3}$ shifted by units.4141 41 These are the hypergeometric analogue of the cosmology shift relations discussed in Section 3.4. That these relations exist becomes a trivial consequence of the finite vector space structure of the space of integrals. In order to make a more direct connection to the Gauss contiguous relations, it is helpful to choose a different normalization of the integrands, and consider instead

$$ \displaystyle F(A,B) \displaystyle\equiv\int_{0}^{\infty}{\rm d}x\frac{x^{\varepsilon_{1}}}{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}(x+X)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\varepsilon_{2}+A}}}{\color[rgb]{0.1719,0.6289,0.1719}(x+1)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\varepsilon_{3}+B}}}}\,, \displaystyle G(A,B) \displaystyle\equiv\int_{0}^{\infty}\frac{{\rm d}x}{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}{x}}\frac{x^{\varepsilon_{1}}}{{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}(x+X)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\varepsilon_{2}+A}}}{\color[rgb]{0.1719,0.6289,0.1719}(x+1)^{{\color[rgb]{0,0,0}\varepsilon_{3}+B}}}}\,, $$

so that $I_{1}=G(1,0)/X$ and $I_{2}=F(1,1)/(1-X)$ . It must be possible to choose any two representatives from $F$ and $G$ and transform all others into this basis. This implies relations between the functions with shifted values of $A$ and $B$ . For example, we can use the identity

$$ \frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{x+X}-\frac{X}{x(x+X)}=0\,, $$

to derive such relations by integrating. We know that

$$ \int_{0}^{\infty}{\rm d}x\frac{x^{\varepsilon_{1}}}{(x+X)^{\varepsilon_{2}+A}(x+1)^{\varepsilon_{3}+B}}\left[\frac{1}{x}-\frac{1}{x+X}-\frac{X}{x(x+X)}\right]=0\,. $$

Translating this into a statement about the integrals (A.78), we find

$$ G(A,B)-F(A+1,B)-XG(A+1,B)=0\,. $$

Employing similar partial fraction identities, we can also derive the shift relations

$$ \displaystyle G(A,B)-F(A,B+1)-G(A,B+1) \displaystyle=0\,, \displaystyle F(A+1,B)-F(A,B+1)-(1-X)F(A+1,B+1) \displaystyle=0\,. $$

Finally, we can use the total derivative relation4242 42 The total derivative of the integrand of $G$ diverges at $x=0$ and so does not lead to an interesting relation.

$$ \int_{0}^{\infty}{\rm d}\left(\frac{x^{\varepsilon_{1}}}{(x+X)^{\varepsilon_{2}+A}(x+1)^{\varepsilon_{3}+B}}\right)=0\,, $$

to infer the relation

$$ \varepsilon_{1}G(A,B)-(\varepsilon_{2}+A)F(A+1,B)-(\varepsilon_{3}+B)F(A,B+1)=0\,. $$

One can prove that the shift relations (A.81), (A.82) and (A.84) are sufficient to transform any element of the integral family into a chosen basis, and so all other shift relations can be obtained from these identities. These relations can be translated into a more familiar form by using the relation between the functions $F$ and $G$ and the hypergeometric function. Note that these shift relations can be used to derive the differential equation (A.72) in a more brute-force way: one just differentiates the basis elements, and then uses the shift relations to rewrite the result back in the original basis. Since the vector space is finite dimensional, this always has to be possible and leads to a differential equation for the basis functions.

As before, we have organized the tubings by the number of vertices enclosed by tubes that also contain a cross. This separates the functions into the sources that appear at each level of the differential equations. To label the large number of functions, we are forced to introduce a slightly cumbersome index notation. The functions in the second column each only have one tube that contains crosses. Their first subscript is the vertex associated to this tube. The labels $1$ and $4$ are assigned to the tubings around the end vertices, whereas the notation $i_{r}$ for $r\in\{1,2,3\}$ indicate the three different ways we can draw tubings encircling an inner vertex $i\in\{2,3\}$ . The multiple subscript labels in the other columns then mean a union of these “elementary” tubes. This composition is independent of the ordering, so that e.g. $F_{41}=F_{14}$ .

The total number of functions in this example is

$$ 1\ +\ 8\ +\ 22\ +\ 24\ +\ 9\ =\ 64\,, $$

so the basis is 64-dimensional. This number is consistent with the general formula $4^{e}$ , where $e=3$ is the number of edges of the graph. Adding the number of functions with alternating signs, we again find $1-8+22-24+9=0$ . We will present the differential equations for a representative subset of these functions.

Again, we have an instance of an activated tube growing twice by absorbing a neighboring tube, but it works just as in (B.11) and is completely predicted by the graphical rules.

### B.2 Four-Site Star

Another interesting test case is the four-site star; cf. (2.33). In this case, there is not enough room for complicated merger and absorption phenomena, so the equations will actually be simpler than those for the four-site chain.

We leave it as an exercise to the reader to draw the set of complete tubings of the marked four-site star (see (4.60) for some examples). There are now 10 tubings encircling a single vertex in tubes that also contain a cross, $24$ tubings with $2$ encircled vertices, $23$ tubings with $3$ encircled vertices and finally $7$ tubings with $4$ encircled vertices. The total number of basis functions is

$$ 1\ +\ 10\ +\ 24\ +\ 22\ +\ 7\ =\ 64\,, $$

and their alternating sum again vanishes

$$ 1\ -\ 10\ +\ 24\ -\ 22\ +\ 7\ =\ 0\,.\phantom{1} $$

## Appendix C Integrability from Locality

An important (and nontrivial) feature of the graphical rules presented in Section 5 is that they imply that ${\rm d}^{2}=0$ . This is required for consistency/integrability of the differential equations, and motivates this graphical procedure from an abstract perspective. Given a cochain complex, with a differential defined in some way, it is natural to study the cohomology of this complex and understand its features. In principle, this would provide a completely orthogonal starting point that would lead us to the study of the same set of equations.

In this appendix, we will to describe how the graphical rules guarantee that ${\rm d}^{2}=0$ , and to explore both the rigidity of the construction, and its relation to spacetime locality.

Versions of these relations exist for all graphs and all ways of splitting tubes into smaller pieces. We can understand the consequences of these relations geometrically. In the space of kinematic variables, each letter can be thought of as defining a hyperplane, the three-letter relations imply the incidence of three of these hyperplanes along a codimension-two surface. This degeneration implies that the canonical form (written in ${\rm d}\log$ form) vanishes, implying relations between wedge products of ${\rm d}\log$ forms. As we will see, ${\rm d}^{2}$ of a function is always proportional to these identically zero combinations.

- • The other nontrivial feature is the precise assignment of functions and signs to the graphical rules. To illustrate this, recall the tree structure (5.39) of the function $Q_{1}$ for the three-site chain: $Q_{1}$ $q_{1}$ $\tilde{q}_{3}$ $(-\tilde{q}_{2})$ (C.3) In addition to the functions being assigned to the corresponding graph tubings in the tree, there were two noteworthy aspects of the rules: i) the subtraction of each immediate descendant from its parent function and ii) the sign of the descendant functions given by $(-1)^{N_{a}}$ , with $N_{a}$ being the number of absorptions along the path from the original graph. To elucidate the necessity of these features, we will consider a modified version of the graphical rules that leads to the following differential equation for $Q_{1}$ : $\displaystyle{\rm d}Q_{1}=\varepsilon\,\Big[Q_{1}\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\includegraphics[]{Figures/Tubings/three/letters/LLbmp.pdf}}\,+\,(Q_{1}-{\color[rgb]{0.3516,0,0.4688}c_{S}}\hskip 1.0ptq_{1})$ $\displaystyle\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\includegraphics[]{Figures/Tubings/three/letters/LLap.pdf}}\,+\,\ \ (Q_{1}-{\color[rgb]{0.3516,0,0.4688}c_{S}}\hskip 1.0pt\tilde{q}_{3})\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\includegraphics[]{Figures/Tubings/three/letters/LLcp.pdf}}\phantom{\Big]}$ (C.4) $\displaystyle+\ q_{1}$ $\displaystyle\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\includegraphics[]{Figures/Tubings/three/letters/LLabpr.pdf}}\,+\,(\tilde{q}_{3}+{\color[rgb]{1,0.6016,0.1992}c_{A}}{\color[rgb]{0.3516,0,0.4688}c_{S}}\hskip 1.0pt\tilde{q}_{2})\raisebox{-3.0pt}{\includegraphics[]{Figures/Tubings/three/letters/LLcm.pdf}}\phantom{\Big]}$ $\displaystyle-\ {\color[rgb]{1,0.6016,0.1992}c_{A}}\hskip 1.0pt\tilde{q}_{2}\ \raisebox{-3.0pt}{\includegraphics[]{Figures/Tubings/three/letters/LLbcmb.pdf}}\Big]$ where the coefficient ${\color[rgb]{0.3516,0,0.4688}c_{S}}$ parameterizes the subtraction of descendants and ${\color[rgb]{1,0.6016,0.1992}c_{A}}$ is an extra grading for functions created by absorption. In what follows, we illustrate through examples that ${c_{S}=c_{A}=1}$ is a consequence of the integrability of our differential equations.

We will now show how these two features guarantee that ${\rm d}^{2}=0$ in a nontrivial way.

### C.2 Two-Site Chain

We first consider the example of the two-site chain. In that case, the three-letter relations shown in (C.2) imply the following identities between triplets of dlog forms:

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}R_{1}}&\equiv\partial[\hat{B}_{2}\hat{B}_{3}\hat{B}_{4}]=-[\hat{B}_{3}\hat{B}_{4}]+[\hat{B}_{2}\hat{B}_{4}]-[\hat{B}_{2}\hat{B}_{3}]=0\,,\\
{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}R_{2}}&\equiv\partial[\hat{B}_{1}\hat{B}_{3}\hat{B}_{5}]=-[\hat{B}_{3}\hat{B}_{5}]+[\hat{B}_{1}\hat{B}_{5}]-[\hat{B}_{1}\hat{B}_{3}]=0\,,\end{split} $$

where $[\hat{B}_{i}\hat{B}_{j}]\equiv{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{i}\wedge{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{j}$ .

The modified graphical rules (C.4) give the following differential equations for the two-site chain:

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}\psi \displaystyle=\varepsilon\big[(\psi-{\color[rgb]{0.3516,0,0.4688}c_{S}}F)\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{1}+F\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{4}+(\psi-{\color[rgb]{0.3516,0,0.4688}c_{S}}\tilde{F})\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{2}+\tilde{F}\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{5}\big]\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}F \displaystyle=\varepsilon\big[F\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{4}+(F-{\color[rgb]{0.3516,0,0.4688}c_{S}}Z)\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{2}+Z\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{3}\big]\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}\tilde{F} \displaystyle=\varepsilon\big[\tilde{F}\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{5}+(\tilde{F}-{\color[rgb]{0.3516,0,0.4688}c_{S}}Z)\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{1}+Z\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{3}\big]\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}Z \displaystyle=2\varepsilon\hskip 1.0ptZ\hskip 1.0pt{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{3}\,. $$

Taking a further differential of these equations, we get

$$ \displaystyle\begin{split}{\rm d}^{2}\psi&=\varepsilon^{2}\Big[Z({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}R_{1}}+{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}R_{2}})+(1-{\color[rgb]{0.3516,0,0.4688}c_{S}})\Big(Z\big[{\rm d}\log(\hat{B}_{3}/\hat{B}_{5})\wedge{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{1}-{\rm d}\log(\hat{B}_{3}/\hat{B}_{4})\wedge{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{2}\big]\\
&\hskip 85.35826pt+F\,{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{4}\wedge{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{1}+\tilde{F}\,{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{5}\wedge{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{2}\Big)\Big]\,,\end{split} \displaystyle{\rm d}^{2}F \displaystyle=\varepsilon^{2}Z\Big[{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}R_{1}}+(1-{\color[rgb]{0.3516,0,0.4688}c_{S}})\,{\rm d}\log(2\hat{B}_{3}/\hat{B}_{4})\wedge{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{2}\Big]\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}^{2}\tilde{F} \displaystyle=\varepsilon^{2}Z\Big[{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}R_{2}}+(1-{\color[rgb]{0.3516,0,0.4688}c_{S}})\,{\rm d}\log(2\hat{B}_{3}/\hat{B}_{5})\wedge{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{1}\Big]\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}^{2}Z \displaystyle=0\,. $$

Note that there are non-vanishing combinations of ${\rm d}\log$ forms proportional to $1-c_{S}$ . Integrability of these equations then forces $c_{S}=1$ . (Since this system does not have any absorptions, we get no constraint on $c_{A}$ , as expected.) The assignment of source functions in (C.6)—including their signs—is then precisely such that the ${\rm d}^{2}$ of all functions is proportional to the vanishing three-letter identities in (C.5). Note that ${\rm d}^{2}\psi$ contains $R_{1}+R_{2}$ because there are two ways of reaching the function $Z$ . Graphically, we can represent this as

$$ \psi F \tilde{F} Z 1 2 $$

As we will see, this tree structure will arise locally in more complicated examples.

$$ \displaystyle R_{1} \displaystyle\equiv\partial[\hat{B}_{4}\hat{B}_{5}\hat{B}_{11}]=0\,, \displaystyle R_{2} \displaystyle\equiv\partial[\hat{B}_{3}\hat{B}_{4}\hat{B}_{12}]=0\,, \displaystyle R_{3} \displaystyle\equiv\partial[\hat{B}_{4}\hat{B}_{6}\hat{B}_{7}]=0\,, \displaystyle R_{4} \displaystyle\equiv\partial[\hat{B}_{1}\hat{B}_{4}\hat{B}_{13}]=0\,, \displaystyle R_{5} \displaystyle\equiv\partial[\hat{B}_{2}\hat{B}_{5}\hat{B}_{7}]=0\,, \displaystyle R_{6} \displaystyle\equiv\partial[\hat{B}_{1}\hat{B}_{5}\hat{B}_{8}]=0\,, \displaystyle R_{7} \displaystyle\equiv\partial[\hat{B}_{7}\hat{B}_{9}\hat{B}_{12}]=0\,, \displaystyle R_{8} \displaystyle\equiv\partial[\hat{B}_{1}\hat{B}_{10}\hat{B}_{12}]=0\,, \displaystyle R_{9} \displaystyle\equiv\partial[\hat{B}_{2}\hat{B}_{6}\hat{B}_{11}]=0\,, \displaystyle R_{10} \displaystyle\equiv\partial[\hat{B}_{3}\hat{B}_{6}\hat{B}_{9}]=0\,, \displaystyle R_{11} \displaystyle\equiv\partial[\hat{B}_{8}\hat{B}_{11}\hat{B}_{13}]=0\,, \displaystyle R_{12} \displaystyle\equiv\partial[\hat{B}_{3}\hat{B}_{10}\hat{B}_{13}]=0\,, $$

where $[\hat{B}_{i}\hat{B}_{j}\hat{B}_{k}]\equiv{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{i}\wedge{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{j}\wedge{\rm d}\log\hat{B}_{k}$ .

Computing ${\rm d}^{2}\psi$ with the modified graphical rules (C.4), we find

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}^{2}\psi \displaystyle=\varepsilon^{2}\Big[q_{1}({\color[rgb]{0.6992,0.3984,1}R_{5}}+{\color[rgb]{0.1719,0.6289,0.1719}R_{6}})+q_{2}({\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}R_{7}}-{\color[rgb]{0.1211,0.4648,0.707}R_{8}})-\tilde{q}_{2}({\color[rgb]{0.75,0.5,0.25}R_{11}}+{\color[rgb]{1,0.6016,0.1992}R_{12}})+\tilde{q}_{1}({\color[rgb]{0.3516,0,0.4688}R_{9}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,0.5}R_{10}})\Big]+\cdots\,, $$

where the ellipsis denotes non-vanishing combinations of dlog forms that are proportional to $1-c_{S}$ , $1-c_{A}$ and $1-c_{A}c_{S}$ . Integrability then forces $c_{S}=c_{A}=1$ .

After imposing these conditions, we see that integrability is related to the identities in (C.13). Graphically, we express this as

$$ \psi Q_{2} F \tilde{F} Q_{1} Q_{3} q_{1} q_{2} \tilde{q}_{2} \tilde{q}_{1} 7 8 12 11 6 5 10 9 $$

Inspection of (C.12) naturally explains that appearance to the relevant three-letter relations. Each identity corresponds to a splitting of the letters associated to the source functions $q_{1,2}$ and $\tilde{q}_{1,2}$ .

The ${\rm d}^{2}$ of the functions $F$ and $\tilde{F}$ is

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}^{2}F \displaystyle=\varepsilon^{2}\Big[q_{1}\hskip 1.0pt{\color[rgb]{0.6992,0.3984,1}R_{5}}+q_{2}\hskip 1.0pt{\color[rgb]{0.8398,0.1523,0.1563}R_{7}}+\tilde{g}({\color[rgb]{0.3516,0,0.4688}R_{9}}+{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,0.5}R_{10}})+Z({\color[rgb]{0.3,0.4,0.9}R_{2}}-{\color[rgb]{0.65,0.2,0.2}R_{1}})\Big]=0\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}^{2}\tilde{F} \displaystyle=\varepsilon^{2}\Big[\tilde{q}_{1}\hskip 1.0pt{\color[rgb]{0.3516,0,0.4688}R_{9}}+\tilde{q}_{2}\hskip 1.0pt{\color[rgb]{0.75,0.5,0.25}R_{11}}+g({\color[rgb]{0.6992,0.3984,1}R_{5}}+{\color[rgb]{0.1719,0.6289,0.1719}R_{6}})+Z({\color[rgb]{1,0,1}R_{4}}-{\color[rgb]{0.38,1,0.88}R_{3}})\Big]=0\,. $$

Graphically, the result in (C.15) corresponds to

$$ F \tilde{F} q_{2} q_{1} q_{3} f \tilde{q}_{2} \tilde{q}_{1} \tilde{q}_{3} f Z \tilde{g} g 2 4 1 3 7 5 11 9 6 5 10 9 $$

Each labelled line again corresponds to a specific splitting of the letters associated to the source functions. Somewhat remarkably, the functions whose letters do not have a possible three letter relation with the parent function (like $f$ for $F$ ) identically drop out of the ${\rm d}^{2}$ equation, while those that do have three letter relations appear, but proportional to the identically vanishing combination. (We saw a similar phenomenon for $\psi$ , where $Q_{i},F,\tilde{F}$ did not appear in ${\rm d}^{2}\psi$ either.)

The ${\rm d}^{2}$ of the $Q_{i}$ functions is

$$ \displaystyle{\rm d}^{2}Q_{1} \displaystyle=\varepsilon^{2}\Big[q_{1}\hskip 1.0pt{\color[rgb]{0,1,0}R_{6}}-\tilde{q}_{2}\hskip 1.0pt{\color[rgb]{0.75,0.5,0.25}R_{11}}-Z({\color[rgb]{0.65,0.2,0.2}R_{1}}+{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}R_{4}})\Big]=0\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}^{2}Q_{2} \displaystyle=\varepsilon^{2}\Big[-q_{2}\hskip 1.0pt{\color[rgb]{0,0,1}R_{8}}-\tilde{q}_{2}\hskip 1.0pt{\color[rgb]{1,0.39,0.13}R_{12}}+Z({\color[rgb]{0.3,0.4,0.9}R_{2}}+{\color[rgb]{1,0,1}R_{4}})\Big]=0\,, \displaystyle{\rm d}^{2}Q_{3} \displaystyle=\varepsilon^{2}\Big[q_{2}\hskip 1.0pt{\color[rgb]{1,0,0}R_{7}}+\tilde{q}_{1}\hskip 1.0pt{\color[rgb]{0,0.5,0.5}R_{10}}-Z({\color[rgb]{0.3,0.4,0.9}R_{2}}+{\color[rgb]{0.38,1,0.88}R_{3}})\Big]=0\,, $$

$$ f \tilde{g} g q_{2} \tilde{q}_{2} q_{3} \tilde{q}_{3} Z 3 1 9 5 11 6 2 4 7 10 $$
